comparison: Both evaluate claims C1-C6 about zebrafish orthology and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes specific data sources (Ensembl database, evolutionary knowledge), while peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings by describing the work as 'well-written' with 'solid' data.

Both evaluate claims C7-C8 about developmental expression and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval cites specific scRNA-seq data (Raj et al., 2020, Figure 1b), while peer reviewers accept the findings as part of 'comprehensive' phenotypic characterization.

Both evaluate claims C9-C13 about protein sequence conservation and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes C13 is an inference requiring functional validation, while peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as part of 'convincing evidence.'

Both evaluate claims C14-C19 about mutagenesis efficiency and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval details the sequencing data (Figures 3c-d), while peer reviewers accept the F0 knockout approach as 'thorough' and 'well-designed.'

Both evaluate claims C24-C28 about Aβ production and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval cites ELISA data (Figure 3e), while peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the finding that psen1 is 'principally responsible for the generation of AB40 and AB42 in zebrafish.'

Both evaluate claims C33-C39 about morphological phenotypes and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes some claims are inferences from phenotypic data, while peer reviewers accept the 'comprehensive' phenotypic characterization.

Both evaluate claims C40-C44 about psen1 behavioral phenotypes and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval cites behavioral tracking data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b-c), while peer reviewers note psen1 shows 'similar night-time phenotypes' to late-onset genes.

Both evaluate claims C45-C52 about psen2 behavioral phenotypes and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes substantial effect sizes (Figures 3g-h) and correction for pigmentation, while peer reviewers note 'psen-2 mutations increase daytime sleep' and accept the comprehensive correction approach.

Both evaluate claims C53-C59 about appa/appb and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes more subtle behavioral phenotypes than psen2, while peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge 'appa/appb mutations have no impact on sleep.'

Both evaluate claims C60-C66 about comparative findings and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes C64-C66 are appropriately speculative, while peer reviewers accept the observations and cautious mechanistic speculation as part of 'solid' data.

Both evaluate claims C67-C69 about apoea/apoeb and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval cites behavioral tracking data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e), while peer reviewers include this in the finding that 'loss-of-function in late-onset AD genes universally result in nighttime sleep loss.'

Both evaluate claims C70-C71 about cd2ap and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes inconsistent results between clutches except for night phenotype, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the universal nighttime sleep loss finding.

Both evaluate claims C72-C74 about clu and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes night effect sizes were not well replicated across clutches, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the universal nighttime sleep loss finding.

Both evaluate claims C75-C80 about sorl1 behavioral phenotypes and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes distinct day and night phenotypes (Figures 4—figure supplement 4c-d, 5), while peer reviewers praise the 'comprehensive' behavioral characterization.

Both evaluate claims C81-C85 about universal nighttime sleep loss and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval calls this a 'key finding,' while peer reviewers explicitly state findings are 'consistent with the well-supported hypothesis that sleep disruption contributes to Alzheimer's-related pathologies.'

Both evaluate claims C86-C90 about serotonin pathway enrichment but differ in evaluation. OpenEval finds them SUPPORTED by permutation tests (Figures 5a-b), while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting 'exploration of potential mechanisms for serotonin disruption in sorl1 mutants is limited' and questioning whether the connection is strengthened.

Both evaluate claims C91-C94 about fluoxetine response but differ in evaluation. OpenEval finds them SUPPORTED by dose-dependent differential response (Figures 5c-d), while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, stating 'I disagree that the connection between sorl1 and serotonin is strengthened' and noting lack of negative controls.

Both evaluate claims C95-C98 about citalopram response but differ in evaluation. OpenEval finds them SUPPORTED despite opposite responses to two SSRIs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c-d), while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning the interpretation and noting the opposite responses complicate conclusions.

Both evaluate claims C99-C101 about tryptophan hydroxylase expression and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval cites HCR quantification (Figures 5e-f) and scRNA-seq data, while peer reviewers do not directly challenge the molecular findings but note mechanistic exploration is limited.

Both evaluate claims C102-C112 about SORL1/retromer function but differ in evaluation. OpenEval finds C102-C108 SUPPORTED by literature and rates overall UNCERTAIN due to C109-C110 being speculative, while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting the hypothesis about 5-HT2 receptor regulation is 'proposed but not tested' and mechanisms are 'more complicated than suggested.'

Both evaluate claims C115-C118 about betamethasone rescue and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval cites behavioral tracking data (Figures 6b-c), while peer reviewers call this 'an exciting demonstration of the approach,' though one questions whether behavioral normalization indicates mechanism normalization.

Both evaluate claims C119-C121 about the behavioral pharmacology approach but differ in evaluation. OpenEval finds them SUPPORTED as reasonable summaries and inferences, while peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN with mixed views: one finds it 'exciting' but another remains 'unconvinced that this approach will yield valuable therapeutic insights.'

Both evaluate claims C122-C137 about sleep disruption context and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes these are supported by literature citations providing important context, while peer reviewers explicitly note findings are 'consistent with the well-supported hypothesis that sleep disruption contributes to Alzheimer's-related pathologies.'

Both evaluate claims C138-C145 about methodological advances and find them SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative comparisons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a-b), while peer reviewers explicitly praise this, stating 'The addition of an extensive behavioral analysis pipeline is of value to the field' and will 'provide considerable value for zebrafish neuroscientists.'

OpenEval evaluates claims C20-C23 about presenilin function in humans as SUPPORTED by established literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; reviewers did not separately address this background information.

OpenEval evaluates claims C29-C32 about comparative findings in mice and zebrafish as SUPPORTED by literature citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; reviewers did not separately address this comparative context.

OpenEval evaluates claims C50-C52 about psen2 behavioral correction for pigmentation as SUPPORTED (Figure 3—figure supplement 3c-e). Peer reviewers addressed broader psen2 phenotypes (R8) but did not separately evaluate the pigmentation correction analysis.

OpenEval evaluates claims C109-C112 about SORL1/5-HT2 receptor speculation as UNCERTAIN, noting it requires experimental validation. Peer reviewers addressed overlapping claims in R19 but did not separately evaluate this specific mechanistic speculation.

OpenEval evaluates claims C113-C114 about therapeutic relevance of serotonin modulation as SUPPORTED by literature citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; reviewers did not separately address this therapeutic context.

OpenEval evaluates claims C132-C137 about contextualizing sleep findings within AD literature as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers addressed broader contextualization (R22) but did not separately evaluate these specific discussion points about infant sleep patterns and AD literature.
